A gs$=$8 ablation demonstrates that increasing group size does not resolve the failure, but larger group sizes remain unexplored. All GRPO experiments truncate completions at 256 tokens (80--84\% truncation); all conditions share this setting, so relative comparisons are fair, but absolute conclusions about $\dsyc$ reward utility may be affected. Truncation analysis confirms this concern: $\dsyc$ AUROC drops from 0.76 (full response) to 0.60 (256 tokens).

3	Our evaluation uses the same 181 prompt pairs for both training and evaluation. While this is controlled across methods (GRPO also trains on identical prompts), the absolute $\sycon$ values should be interpreted as on-distribution performance. To verify generalization, we retrain ACT on a stratified 80/20 split (146/35 pair IDs, ensuring no pair appears in both sets). The held-out model achieves $\sycon{=}0.204$ on the 20\% unseen pairs ($n{=}35$) after only 500 training steps, compared to 0.056 for the vanilla baseline---a $3.7{\times}$ improvement. This reaches 72\% of the reference ceiling (0.284) established by the full-data model on the same subset, confirming that ACT's gains generalize beyond the training set.
4	
5	Our RL training uses Qwen3-8B exclusively; cross-model discriminability is confirmed on Llama-3-8B (AUROC $0.779$; Table~\ref{tab:cross_model}), but compute constraints prevented training replication on a second architecture.

Our GRPO experiments use group sizes of 2 and 8, below the typical range of 8--64 \citep{shao2024grpo}. A gs$=$8 ablation demonstrates that increasing group size does not resolve the failure, but larger group sizes remain unexplored. All GRPO experiments truncate completions at 256 tokens (80--84\% truncation); all conditions share this setting, so relative comparisons are fair, but absolute conclusions about $\dsyc$ reward utility may be affected. Truncation analysis confirms this concern: $\dsyc$ AUROC drops from 0.76 (full response) to 0.60 (256 tokens).

Our evaluation uses the same 181 prompt pairs for both training and evaluation. While this is controlled across methods (GRPO also trains on identical prompts), the absolute $\sycon$ values should be interpreted as on-distribution performance. To verify generalization, we retrain ACT on a stratified 80/20 split (146/35 pair IDs, ensuring no pair appears in both sets). The held-out model achieves $\sycon{=}0.204$ on the 20\% unseen pairs ($n{=}35$) after only 500 training steps, compared to 0.056 for the vanilla baseline---a $3.7{\times}$ improvement. This reaches 72\% of the reference ceiling (0.284) established by the full-data model on the same subset, confirming that ACT's gains generalize beyond the training set.

Our RL training uses Qwen3-8B exclusively; cross-model discriminability is confirmed on Llama-3-8B (AUROC $0.779$; Table~\ref{tab:cross_model}), but compute constraints prevented training replication on a second architecture.

All GRPO experiments truncate completions at 256 tokens (80--84\% truncation); all conditions share this setting, so relative comparisons are fair, but absolute conclusions about $\dsyc$ reward utility may be affected. Our evaluation uses the same 181 prompt pairs for both training and evaluation. While this is controlled across methods (GRPO also trains on identical prompts), the absolute $\sycon$ values should be interpreted as on-distribution performance. To verify generalization, we retrain ACT on a stratified 80/20 split (146/35 pair IDs, ensuring no pair appears in both sets). The held-out model achieves $\sycon{=}0.204$ on the 20\% unseen pairs ($n{=}35$) after only 500 training steps, compared to 0.056 for the vanilla baseline---a $3.7{\times}$ improvement. Our GRPO experiments use group sizes of 2 and 8, below the typical range of 8--64 \citep{shao2024grpo}. A gs$=$8 ablation demonstrates that increasing group size does not resolve the failure, but larger group sizes remain unexplored. All GRPO experiments truncate completions at 256 tokens (80--84\% truncation); all conditions share this setting, so relative comparisons are fair, but absolute conclusions about $\dsyc$ reward utility may be affected. Truncation analysis confirms this concern: $\dsyc$ AUROC drops from 0.76 (full response) to 0.60 (256 tokens).

Our evaluation uses the same 181 prompt pairs for both training and evaluation. While this is controlled across methods (GRPO also trains on identical prompts), the absolute $\sycon$ values should be interpreted as on-distribution performance. To verify generalization, we retrain ACT on a stratified 80/20 split (146/35 pair IDs, ensuring no pair appears in both sets). The held-out model achieves $\sycon{\approx}0.20$ on the 20\% unseen pairs ($n{=}35$) across three checkpoints (steps 500, 1000, 1500), a $3.7{\times}$ improvement over the vanilla baseline (0.056). Performance saturates early, reaching 72\% of the reference ceiling established by the full-data model (0.284) on the same subset. This confirms that ACT's gains generalize beyond the training set, though the 28\% gap suggests partial reliance on training-set-specific patterns.

Our RL training uses Qwen3-8B exclusively; cross-model discriminability is confirmed on Llama-3-8B (AUROC $0.779$; Table~\ref{tab:cross_model}), but compute constraints prevented training replication on a second architecture.

\section{When Does Discriminability Fail as Reward Utility?}\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Root cause of the probe reward trap.}
The probe reward trap (\S\ref{sec:probe_trap}) and the cosine failures (\S\ref{sec:cosine_failure}) share a common geometric root.
$\dsyc$ encodes the \emph{direction} of belief change but not its \emph{evidential warrant}: valid revision and sycophantic capitulation both shift activations toward the user's position along the same direction.
The two reward families expose complementary faces of this blindness.
Cosine $\rone$ penalizes all belief change indiscriminately; the resulting mode collapse (F1c, F1d) reflects excessive punishment of any activation shift along $\dsyc$.
The binary probe $\rone$ rewards all resistance regardless of input validity; the stubbornness trap ($\tof = 0$ by step 500) reflects excessive permissiveness toward activation stasis.
These are not independent design flaws but dual consequences of a direction that conflates the target behavior (resisting invalid challenges) with its complement (refusing valid corrections).
Cross-model evidence confirms the limitation extends beyond Qwen3-8B: Llama-3-8B independently achieves AUROC $0.779$ (bootstrap 95\% CI $[0.745,\, 0.819]$) on the same contrastive pairs with the same monotonic evidence gradient, so discriminability generalizes across architectures while the semantic gap between discriminability and reward utility persists.
This pattern contrasts with reasoning faithfulness and safety directions~\citep{zhang2026latentgrpo}, where the behavior to suppress is geometrically distinct from the behavior to preserve along the relevant direction.
\citet{wu2026rewardhacking} reinforce this principle: concept directions applied via advantage modification in GRPO achieve 100\% validation accuracy for reward hacking detection, where shortcut behaviors are geometrically separable.
A quantitative comparison of geometric separability between $\dsyc$ and their reward-hacking directions remains an important open question.
For sycophancy, the target and its complement occupy the same activation region; they differ only in whether external evidence warrants the belief change.

\paragraph{GRPO results under our configuration.}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Comparison of all sycophancy calibration methods on Qwen3-8B. $\sycon$ is the harmonic mean of $\tof$ and $\nof$; higher indicates better calibration. Best result in \textbf{bold}. $^\dagger$Best checkpoint (seed 1, step 6500); only 4/28 checkpoints across two seeds exceed vanilla. $^\ddagger$Seed 2 (16 checkpoints); all exceed vanilla. Best $\sycon{=}0.286$ (step 7000). $^\S$All cosine variants collapsed from step 1 ($\tof{=}0$ at every checkpoint); F1d additionally diverged at step 2160 (entropy ${<}\,0.01$). $^\P$ACT and ActAdd differ from GRPO along 5+ dimensions (\S\ref{sec:discussion}); included for context, not as controlled comparisons.}
\label{tab:main_comparison}
\begin{tabular}{llcccc}
\toprule
Method & Type & $\sycon$ $\uparrow$ & $\tof$ $\uparrow$ & $\nof$ $\uparrow$ & Step \\
\midrule
Vanilla & -- & 0.134 & 0.072 & 0.945 & -- \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{6}{l}{\textit{GRPO with $\dsyc$}} \\
Cosine $\rone$ (F1a--F1d) & RL & 0.000$^\S$ & 0.000 & 1.000 & 500 \\
Continuous Probe $\rone$ (F3) & RL & 0.124 & 0.066 & 0.934 & 500 \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{6}{l}{\textit{SFT with $\dsyc$ probe penalty}} \\
Binary Probe $\rone$ (F2) & SFT & 0.000 & 0.000 & 0.995 & 500 \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{6}{l}{\textit{GRPO without $\dsyc$}} \\
$\rthree$-only GRPO & RL & 0.153$^\dagger$ & 0.083 & 0.983 & 6500 \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{6}{l}{\textit{Reference methods (not directly comparable)$^\P$}} \\
ActAdd ($\alpha{=}5$) & Inference & 0.054 & 0.028 & 0.961 & -- \\
\textbf{ACT} (seed 1) & SFT & \textbf{0.301} & \textbf{0.182} & 0.867 & 8000 \\
ACT (seed 2)$^\ddagger$ & SFT & 0.286 & -- & -- & 7000 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Table~\ref{tab:main_comparison} summarizes all methods evaluated on Qwen3-8B.
$\rthree$-only GRPO removes $\dsyc$ entirely and relies on the NLI-based behavioral reward alone.
If the failures in Sections~\ref{sec:cosine_failure} and~\ref{sec:probe_trap} stemmed solely from the representation reward, this ablation should recover calibration quality.
It does not.
The $\sycon$ trajectory for $\rthree$-only GRPO oscillates without sustained improvement.
Seed 1 peaks at 0.153 (checkpoint 6500) and ends at 0.143 (checkpoint 8000); seed 2 peaks at 0.143 (checkpoint 4000, its only checkpoint exceeding vanilla) and ends at 0.124 (checkpoint 8000).
Only 4 of 28 checkpoints across both seeds exceed vanilla (14.3\%): 3/12 for seed 1 (25\%) and 1/16 for seed 2 (6.3\%), while ACT exceeds vanilla at every evaluated checkpoint (32/32 across two seeds; Figure~\ref{fig:trajectory}).
Both seeds exhibit oscillations of similar amplitude ($\Delta \approx 0.069$) with crash onset differing by ${\sim}2{,}500$ steps, indicating stochastic drift in a saturated reward landscape.
Activation analysis confirms the drift is not representational: $\dsyc$ AUROC varies by ${<}0.01$ across checkpoints and $\rthree$ saturates at ${\sim}0.98$ ($p{=}0.703$), yet $\sycon$ swings by 17\%, reinforcing the disconnect between discriminability and behavioral utility.
Under our configuration (group size$=$2), $\rthree$-only GRPO exhibits a similar stubbornness pattern to the $\dsyc$ approaches (high $\nof$, near-zero $\tof$) at milder severity.

\paragraph{Competing hypotheses and ablation.}
Three explanations are consistent with our GRPO results: (a)~$\dsyc$ is fundamentally unsuitable as a reward signal for sycophancy calibration; (b)~GRPO with group size$=$2 provides insufficient ranking diversity for any reward to achieve stable calibration; (c)~sycophancy calibration is inherently unsuitable for scalar per-completion RL.
Two ablations address these hypotheses (Table~\ref{tab:ablation}).
Increasing group size from 2 to 8 does not improve $\rthree$-only GRPO: three checkpoints showed a monotonically declining trajectory ($0.084 \to 0.085 \to 0.054$), all below vanilla, and gs$=$8 underperforms gs$=$2 at matched checkpoints (0.084 vs.\ 0.116 at step 500); the experiment was terminated early.
This rules out hypothesis~(b) as the primary explanation.
Reducing ACT's LoRA configuration to match GRPO's (rank 64, $\alpha{=}64$, 4 modules) yields $\sycon = 0.267$ (peak 0.326 at step 7000); all 16 checkpoints exceed vanilla.
Under identical LoRA configurations, per-token SFT ($\sycon{=}0.267$) exceeds per-completion GRPO ($\sycon{=}0.085$) by $3.1{\times}$; supervision granularity is the primary driver, while LoRA capacity modulates convergence rate but is not the determining factor.
The probe reward trap (C2) provides independent evidence for~(a): it arises under SFT where group size is irrelevant.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Ablation: isolating supervision paradigm from LoRA configuration. All methods use Qwen3-8B with $\rthree$ (behavioral reward). Vanilla $\sycon{=}0.134$. $^\dagger$Terminated early after three checkpoints showed monotonically declining trajectory. $^\ddagger$Final checkpoint (step 8000); peak $\sycon{=}0.326$ at step 7000.}
\label{tab:ablation}
\begin{tabular}{llcc}
\toprule
Method & LoRA config & Best $\sycon$ & ${>}$Van. \\
\midrule
GRPO gs$=$2 (2 seeds) & r64, $\alpha$64, 4m & 0.116 & 4/28 \\
GRPO gs$=$8$^\dagger$ & r64, $\alpha$64, 4m & 0.085 & 0/3 \\
\midrule
ACT reduced-LoRA$^\ddagger$ & r64, $\alpha$64, 4m & 0.267 & 16/16 \\
ACT full s1 & r64, $\alpha$128, 7m & 0.301 & 16/16 \\
ACT full s2 & r64, $\alpha$128, 7m & 0.286 & 16/16 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/fig_trajectory.pdf}
\caption{$\sycon$ trajectories for $\rthree$-only GRPO (two seeds) and ACT (two seeds) over training steps. ACT exceeds vanilla at every evaluated checkpoint (32/32 across two seeds); $\rthree$-only GRPO exceeds vanilla at only 4/28 checkpoints (14.3\%).}
\label{fig:trajectory}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{ACT vs.\ GRPO.}
ACT~\citep{consistency2025bctact} achieves $\sycon = 0.301$ (seed 1) and $0.286$ (seed 2) at their respective peaks, more than $2{\times}$ vanilla and above every GRPO variant (Table~\ref{tab:main_comparison}) (held-out validation confirms generalization; see Limitations).
The trajectory is not monotonic---seed 1 dips to 0.214 at step 4000 but self-recovers by step 6000, unlike GRPO where stubbornness persists.
Full ACT peaks around steps 7000--8000 while reduced-LoRA surges to 0.326 at step 7000; both variants maintain above-vanilla performance throughout.
The reduced-LoRA ablation (Table~\ref{tab:ablation}) partially disentangles the five confounding dimensions: with LoRA capacity controlled, per-token SFT still dominates, indicating that supervision granularity---not adapter capacity---is the primary factor.

\paragraph{Relationship to inference-time probe methods.}
\citet{papadatos2024probepenalties} successfully reduce sycophancy using a probe of comparable quality (94\% accuracy) via Best-of-N reranking, where the probe selects among candidates without producing gradients.
Together with our results, this suggests two orthogonal failure dimensions: (1)~inside vs.\ outside the optimization loop---gradient exploitation enables the probe reward trap (\S\ref{sec:probe_trap}), while inference-time reranking sidesteps it; and (2)~scalar per-completion reward---the failure persists even without the probe ($\rthree$-only GRPO), consistent with per-completion information compression as an independent factor.

\paragraph{Future directions.}
Condition-aware rewards, hybrid SFT-then-RL pipelines, and per-step process rewards offer paths forward; whether other REINFORCE-style methods or behavioral attributes with similar geometric entanglement~\citep{skalse2022hacking} exhibit the same failures remains open.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Representation engineering \citep{zou2023repe} reveals that large language models encode sycophancy as a linear direction in their residual streams.
A contrastive sycophancy direction $\dsyc$, extracted from style-controlled pairs of valid belief revision and sycophantic capitulation, achieves cross-validated AUROC $0.827$ on Qwen3-8B and $0.779$ on Llama-3-8B, with discriminability rising monotonically across evidence-strength levels (\S\ref{sec:direction_quality}), though 256-token truncation during GRPO training degrades this to approximately 0.60 (\S\ref{sec:cosine_failure}).
These results point to an appealing possibility: if the model's representations already separate sycophantic from non-sycophantic behavior, that separation should be convertible into a training signal.
Sycophancy is among the most persistent alignment failures in deployed systems \citep{sharma2023sycophancy}, and a representation-level signal could target the internal computation rather than its surface outputs.

This paper documents the \emph{probe reward trap}: when a frozen linear probe on $\dsyc$ is used as an SFT training signal with stopped gradients, behavioral death ($\tof = 0$) occurs within 500 steps while generation entropy remains healthy (0.70), masking the failure from standard monitoring (\S\ref{sec:probe_trap}).
In our experiments, the 1{,}300-step lag before distributional collapse means entropy-based early stopping---the most common safeguard against reward hacking \citep{casper2023openproblems}---would miss the failure entirely, with the reward averaging $+0.72$ throughout.
Because the trap arises under SFT rather than GRPO, it reflects a limitation of $\dsyc$ itself: the direction encodes \emph{whether} belief changed, not \emph{whether it should have}, so any reward conditioned on it alone will either be gamed or reward rigidity.

Under our GRPO configuration (Qwen3-8B, group size$=$2), two additional $\dsyc$-based formulations---cosine projection (\S\ref{sec:cosine_failure}) and continuous probe---also produced behavioral collapse.
Removing $\dsyc$ entirely, $\rthree$-only GRPO (behavioral reward alone) exceeded vanilla at only 4 of 28 checkpoints across two seeds; increasing group size to 8 does not improve performance ($\sycon = 0.085$, below vanilla).
ACT \citep{consistency2025bctact} (dense per-token SFT) exceeds vanilla at every evaluated checkpoint (32/32 across two seeds; \S\ref{sec:discussion}), and a LoRA-controlled ablation isolates supervision granularity as the primary factor.

The root cause is a semantic gap between discriminability and reward utility.
Techniques for discovering latent knowledge \citep{burns2023ccs} and representation-guided RL \citep{zhang2026latentgrpo} share a premise: a direction with high discriminability should transfer into a useful training signal.
For reasoning faithfulness and safety directions, this premise holds because the behavior to suppress is geometrically distinct from the behavior to preserve.
Sycophancy violates this condition: capitulation under social pressure and revision under valid evidence produce overlapping activation signatures along $\dsyc$ \citep{wang2025internal, shapira2026amplifies}.
When reward overoptimization \citep{gao2023scaling} operates on a signal that conflates compliance with capitulation, the result is predictable collapse \citep{skalse2022hacking}.

This paper presents a negative result with mechanistic analysis. Our two principal findings:

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{The probe reward trap: behavioral death before distributional collapse} (C2). A frozen binary probe on $\dsyc$ produces behavioral death ($\tof = 0$ at step 500) while entropy remains at 0.70 and the reward averages $+0.72$. In our experiments, the 1{,}300-step lag before distributional collapse renders standard entropy monitoring blind to the failure. Because the trap arises under SFT---not GRPO---it reflects a limitation of the direction itself, not the optimization algorithm (\S\ref{sec:probe_trap}).

\item \textbf{Scalar per-completion RL fails; supervision granularity is the primary factor} (C1). Under GRPO on Qwen3-8B, all three $\dsyc$-based reward formulations produce behavioral collapse (\S\ref{sec:cosine_failure}, \S\ref{sec:probe_trap}), and $\rthree$-only GRPO also fails (4/28 checkpoints ${>}$ vanilla). A group-size ablation (gs$=$8) rules out variance reduction as the bottleneck; a LoRA-controlled comparison demonstrates that per-token SFT ($\sycon{=}0.267$) exceeds per-completion GRPO ($\sycon{=}0.085$) by $3.1{\times}$ under identical adapter configurations (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).
\end{itemize}

- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review changed code for reuse, quality, and efficiency, then fix any issues found.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled remote agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring remote agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Build, debug, and optimize Claude API / Anthropic SDK apps. Apps built with this skill should include prompt caching. Also handles migrating existing Claude API code between Claude model versions (4.5 → 4.6, 4.6 → 4.7, retired-model replacements).
TRIGGER when: code imports `anthropic`/`@anthropic-ai/sdk`; user asks for the Claude API, Anthropic SDK, or Managed Agents; user adds/modifies/tunes a Claude feature (caching, thinking, compaction, tool use, batch, files, citations, memory) or model (Opus/Sonnet/Haiku) in a file; questions about prompt caching / cache hit rate in an Anthropic SDK project.
SKIP: file imports `openai`/other-provider SDK, filename like `*-openai.py`/`*-generic.py`, provider-neutral code, general programming/ML.
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a pull request
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

1	\section{Related Work}\label{sec:related_work}
2	
3	\paragraph{Representation Engineering.}
4	Linear directions in LLM residual streams encode behavioral concepts \citep{zou2023repe}; inference-time methods---ITI \citep{li2023iti}, ActAdd \citep{turner2023actadd}, CAA \citep{rimsky2024caa}---demonstrate that activation geometry suffices for behavioral control \citep{burns2023ccs}.
5	We use the same contrastive extraction as CAA but apply $\dsyc$ as an RL reward, revealing a gap that inference-time work does not encounter.
6	
7	\paragraph{Reward Design and Overoptimization.}
8	Proxy rewards diverge from true objectives under sustained optimization \citep{gao2023scaling}, and reward hacking can escalate to active tampering \citep{denison2024subterfuge}.
9	Our probe trap (\S\ref{sec:probe_trap}) is an extreme instance: the reward actively reinforces degenerate behavior rather than merely being circumvented \citep{skalse2022hacking}.
10	\citet{wu2026rewardhacking} demonstrate that representation-level directions succeed for reward hacking suppression when behaviors are geometrically separable (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).
11	
12	\paragraph{Sycophancy Characterization and Mitigation.}
13	Sycophancy is pervasive in RLHF-trained assistants \citep{sharma2023sycophancy}, amplified by RLHF \citep{shapira2026amplifies}, and traceable to late-layer preference shifts \citep{wang2025internal}; mitigation approaches include synthetic data \citep{wei2024synthetic}, consistency training \citep{consistency2025bctact}, and neuron-level correction \citep{obrien2025fewbadneurons}.
14	Our analysis shows why the step from diagnosis to reward is structurally blocked: $\dsyc$ conflates warranted revision with unwarranted capitulation.
15	
16	\paragraph{Probe-Based Inference-Time Mitigation.}
17	\citet{papadatos2024probepenalties} reduce sycophancy via Best-of-N reranking with linear probe penalties (94\% probe accuracy), where the probe selects among candidates without producing gradients that update model parameters.
18	Our work reveals what happens when a comparable signal (AUROC 0.82) enters the GRPO training loop: the discriminability--utility gap is specific to gradient-based optimization, not to probe quality per se (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).
19	
20	\paragraph{Representation-Guided RL and Process Rewards.}
21	Latent-GRPO \citep{zhang2026latentgrpo} extends GRPO with latent-space rewards for reasoning; CRAFT \citep{luo2026craft} applies representation-level constraints during RL; \citet{sinii2025smallvectors} and \citet{ackermann2026gradreg} study representation dynamics under RL.
22	SMART \citep{beigi2025smart} applies per-step process rewards with MCTS for sycophancy, succeeding where our completion-level scalar rewards fail; the key difference is supervision granularity, as per-step rewards evaluate behavioral transitions at individual reasoning steps rather than compressing an entire completion into a single scalar.
23	This is consistent with ACT's per-token success and suggests that supervision density, not just the choice of reward signal, mediates reward utility for sycophancy calibration.
24	Preference-based methods (DPO \citep{rafailov2023dpo}, KTO \citep{ethayarajh2024kto}) may accommodate $\dsyc$-derived rankings; whether pair-wise optimization avoids the failures we observe remains open.
25

$\dsyc$ encodes the \emph{direction} of belief change but not its \emph{evidential warrant}: valid revision and sycophantic capitulation both shift activations toward the user's position along the same direction.
The two reward families expose complementary faces of this blindness.
Cosine $\rone$ penalizes all belief change indiscriminately; the resulting mode collapse (F1c, F1d) reflects excessive punishment of any activation shift along $\dsyc$.
The binary probe $\rone$ rewards all resistance regardless of input validity; the stubbornness trap ($\tof = 0$ by step 500) reflects excessive permissiveness toward activation stasis.
These are not independent design flaws but dual consequences of a direction that conflates the target behavior (resisting invalid challenges) with its complement (refusing valid corrections).

\section{When Does Discriminability Fail as Reward Utility?}\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Root cause of the probe reward trap.}
The probe reward trap (\S\ref{sec:probe_trap}) and the cosine failures (\S\ref{sec:cosine_failure}) share a common geometric root.
$\dsyc$ encodes the \emph{direction} of belief change but not its \emph{evidential warrant}: valid revision and sycophantic capitulation both shift activations toward the user's position along the same direction.
The two reward families expose complementary faces of this blindness.
Cosine $\rone$ penalizes all belief change indiscriminately; the resulting mode collapse (F1c, F1d) reflects excessive punishment of any activation shift along $\dsyc$.
The binary probe $\rone$ rewards all resistance regardless of input validity; the stubbornness trap ($\tof = 0$ by step 500) reflects excessive permissiveness toward activation stasis.
These are not independent design flaws but dual consequences of a direction that conflates the target behavior (resisting invalid challenges) with its complement (refusing valid corrections).
Cross-model evidence confirms the limitation extends beyond Qwen3-8B: Llama-3-8B independently achieves AUROC $0.779$ (bootstrap 95\% CI $[0.745,\, 0.819]$) on the same contrastive pairs with the same monotonic evidence gradient, so discriminability generalizes across architectures while the semantic gap between discriminability and reward utility persists.
This pattern contrasts with reasoning faithfulness and safety directions~\citep{zhang2026latentgrpo}, where the behavior to suppress is geometrically distinct from the behavior to preserve along the relevant direction.
\citet{wu2026rewardhacking} reinforce this principle: concept directions applied via advantage modification in GRPO achieve 100\% validation accuracy for reward hacking detection, where shortcut behaviors are geometrically separable.
A quantitative comparison of geometric separability between $\dsyc$ and their reward-hacking directions remains an important open question.
For sycophancy, the target and its complement occupy the same activation region; they differ only in whether external evidence warrants the belief change.

+Increasing group size from 2 to 8 does not improve $\rthree$-only GRPO: three checkpoints showed a monotonically declining trajectory ($0.084 \to 0.085 \to 0.054$), all below vanilla, and gs$=$8 (best 0.085) underperforms gs$=$2 (best 0.153); the experiment was terminated early.
This rules out hypothesis~(b) as the primary explanation.
Reducing ACT's LoRA configuration to match GRPO's (rank 64, $\alpha{=}64$, 4 modules) yields $\sycon = 0.267$ (peak 0.326 at step 7000); all 16 checkpoints exceed vanilla.

Under identical LoRA configurations, per-token SFT ($\sycon{=}0.267$) exceeds per-completion GRPO ($\sycon{=}0.085$) by $3.1{\times}$; supervision granularity is the primary driver, while LoRA capacity modulates convergence rate but is not the determining factor.

26	\item \textbf{The probe reward trap: behavioral death before distributional collapse} (C2). A frozen binary probe on $\dsyc$ produces behavioral death ($\tof = 0$ at step 500) while entropy remains at 0.70 and the reward averages $+0.72$. In our experiments, the 1{,}300-step lag before distributional collapse renders standard entropy monitoring blind to the failure. Because the trap arises under SFT---not GRPO---it reflects a limitation of the direction itself, not the optimization algorithm (\S\ref{sec:probe_trap}).

A group-size ablation (gs$=$8) rules out variance reduction as the bottleneck; a LoRA-controlled comparison demonstrates that per-token SFT ($\sycon{=}0.267$) exceeds per-completion GRPO ($\sycon{=}0.085$) by $3.1{\times}$ under identical adapter configurations (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).

\section{When Does Discriminability Fail as Reward Utility?}\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Root cause of the probe reward trap.}
The probe reward trap (\S\ref{sec:probe_trap}) and the cosine failures (\S\ref{sec:cosine_failure}) share a common geometric root.
$\dsyc$ encodes the \emph{direction} of belief change but not its \emph{evidential warrant}: valid revision and sycophantic capitulation both shift activations toward the user's position along the same direction.
The two reward families expose complementary faces of this blindness.
Cosine $\rone$ penalizes all belief change indiscriminately; the resulting mode collapse (F1c, F1d) reflects excessive punishment of any activation shift along $\dsyc$.
The binary probe $\rone$ rewards all resistance regardless of input validity; the stubbornness trap ($\tof = 0$ by step 500) reflects excessive permissiveness toward activation stasis.
These are not independent design flaws but dual consequences of a direction that conflates the target behavior (resisting invalid challenges) with its complement (refusing valid corrections).
Cross-model evidence confirms the limitation extends beyond Qwen3-8B: Llama-3-8B independently achieves AUROC $0.779$ (bootstrap 95\% CI $[0.745,\, 0.819]$) on the same contrastive pairs with the same monotonic evidence gradient, so discriminability generalizes across architectures while the semantic gap between discriminability and reward utility persists.
This pattern contrasts with reasoning faithfulness and safety directions~\citep{zhang2026latentgrpo}, where the behavior to suppress is geometrically distinct from the behavior to preserve along the relevant direction.
\citet{wu2026rewardhacking} reinforce this principle: concept directions applied via advantage modification in GRPO achieve 100\% validation accuracy for reward hacking detection, where shortcut behaviors are geometrically separable.
A quantitative comparison of geometric separability between $\dsyc$ and their reward-hacking directions remains an important open question.
For sycophancy, the target and its complement occupy the same activation region; they differ only in whether external evidence warrants the belief change.

\paragraph{GRPO results under our configuration.}

\midrule

\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Table~\ref{tab:main_comparison} summarizes all methods evaluated on Qwen3-8B.
$\rthree$-only GRPO removes $\dsyc$ entirely and relies on the NLI-based behavioral reward alone.
If the failures in Sections~\ref{sec:cosine_failure} and~\ref{sec:probe_trap} stemmed solely from the representation reward, this ablation should recover calibration quality.
It does not.
The $\sycon$ trajectory for $\rthree$-only GRPO oscillates without sustained improvement.
Seed 1 peaks at 0.153 (checkpoint 6500) and ends at 0.143 (checkpoint 8000); seed 2 peaks at 0.143 (checkpoint 4000, its only checkpoint exceeding vanilla) and ends at 0.124 (checkpoint 8000).
Only 4 of 28 checkpoints across both seeds exceed vanilla (14.3\%): 3/12 for seed 1 (25\%) and 1/16 for seed 2 (6.3\%), while ACT exceeds vanilla at every evaluated checkpoint (32/32 across two seeds; Figure~\ref{fig:trajectory}).
Both seeds exhibit oscillations of similar amplitude ($\Delta \approx 0.069$) with crash onset differing by ${\sim}2{,}500$ steps, indicating stochastic drift in a saturated reward landscape.
Activation analysis confirms the drift is not representational: $\dsyc$ AUROC varies by ${<}0.01$ across checkpoints and $\rthree$ saturates at ${\sim}0.98$ ($p{=}0.703$), yet $\sycon$ swings by 17\%, reinforcing the disconnect between discriminability and behavioral utility.
Under our configuration (group size$=$2), $\rthree$-only GRPO exhibits a similar stubbornness pattern to the $\dsyc$ approaches (high $\nof$, near-zero $\tof$) at milder severity.

\paragraph{Competing hypotheses and ablation.}
Three explanations are consistent with our GRPO results: (a)~$\dsyc$ is fundamentally unsuitable as a reward signal for sycophancy calibration; (b)~GRPO with group size$=$2 provides insufficient ranking diversity for any reward to achieve stable calibration; (c)~sycophancy calibration is inherently unsuitable for scalar per-completion RL.
Two ablations address these hypotheses (Table~\ref{tab:ablation}).
Increasing group size from 2 to 8 does not improve $\rthree$-only GRPO: three checkpoints showed a monotonically declining trajectory ($0.084 \to 0.085 \to 0.054$), all below vanilla, and gs$=$8 (best 0.085) underperforms gs$=$2 (best 0.153); the experiment was terminated early.
This rules out hypothesis~(b) as the primary explanation.
Reducing ACT's LoRA configuration to match GRPO's (rank 64, $\alpha{=}64$, 4 modules) yields $\sycon = 0.267$ (peak 0.326 at step 7000); all 16 checkpoints exceed vanilla.
Under identical LoRA configurations, per-token SFT ($\sycon{=}0.267$) exceeds per-completion GRPO ($\sycon{=}0.085$) by $3.1{\times}$; supervision granularity is the primary driver, while LoRA capacity modulates convergence rate but is not the determining factor.
The probe reward trap (C2) provides independent evidence for~(a): it arises under SFT where group size is irrelevant.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Ablation: isolating supervision paradigm from LoRA configuration. All methods use Qwen3-8B with $\rthree$ (behavioral reward). Vanilla $\sycon{=}0.134$. $^\dagger$Terminated early after three checkpoints showed monotonically declining trajectory. $^\ddagger$Final checkpoint (step 8000); peak $\sycon{=}0.326$ at step 7000.}
\label{tab:ablation}
\begin{tabular}{llcc}
\toprule
Method & LoRA config & Best $\sycon$ & ${>}$Van. \\
\midrule
GRPO gs$=$2 (2 seeds) & r64, $\alpha$64, 4m & 0.153 & 4/28 \\
GRPO gs$=$8$^\dagger$ & r64, $\alpha$64, 4m & 0.085 & 0/3 \\
\midrule
ACT reduced-LoRA$^\ddagger$ & r64, $\alpha$64, 4m & 0.267 & 16/16 \\
ACT full s1 & r64, $\alpha$128, 7m & 0.301 & 16/16 \\
ACT full s2 & r64, $\alpha$128, 7m & 0.286 & 16/16 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/fig_trajectory.pdf}
\caption{$\sycon$ trajectories for $\rthree$-only GRPO (two seeds) and ACT (two seeds) over training steps. ACT exceeds vanilla at every evaluated checkpoint (32/32 across two seeds); $\rthree$-only GRPO exceeds vanilla at only 4/28 checkpoints (14.3\%).}
\label{fig:trajectory}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{ACT vs.\ GRPO.}
ACT~\citep{consistency2025bctact} achieves $\sycon = 0.301$ (seed 1) and $0.286$ (seed 2) at their respective peaks, more than $2{\times}$ vanilla and above every GRPO variant (Table~\ref{tab:main_comparison}) (held-out validation confirms generalization; see Limitations).
The trajectory is not monotonic---seed 1 dips to 0.214 at step 4000 but self-recovers by step 6000, unlike GRPO where stubbornness persists.
Full ACT peaks around steps 7000--8000 while reduced-LoRA surges to 0.326 at step 7000; both variants maintain above-vanilla performance throughout.
The reduced-LoRA ablation (Table~\ref{tab:ablation}) partially disentangles the five confounding dimensions: with LoRA capacity controlled, per-token SFT still dominates, indicating that supervision granularity---not adapter capacity---is the primary factor.

\paragraph{Relationship to inference-time probe methods.}
\citet{papadatos2024probepenalties} successfully reduce sycophancy using a probe of comparable quality (94\% accuracy) via Best-of-N reranking, where the probe selects among candidates without producing gradients.
Together with our results, this suggests two orthogonal failure dimensions: (1)~inside vs.\ outside the optimization loop---gradient exploitation enables the probe reward trap (\S\ref{sec:probe_trap}), while inference-time reranking sidesteps it; and (2)~scalar per-completion reward---the failure persists even without the probe ($\rthree$-only GRPO), consistent with per-completion information compression as an independent factor.

\paragraph{Future directions.}
Condition-aware rewards, hybrid SFT-then-RL pipelines, and per-step process rewards offer paths forward; whether other REINFORCE-style methods or behavioral attributes with similar geometric entanglement~\citep{skalse2022hacking} exhibit the same failures remains open.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Representation engineering \citep{zou2023repe} reveals that large language models encode sycophancy as a linear direction in their residual streams.
A contrastive sycophancy direction $\dsyc$, extracted from style-controlled pairs of valid belief revision and sycophantic capitulation, achieves cross-validated AUROC $0.827$ on Qwen3-8B and $0.779$ on Llama-3-8B, with discriminability rising monotonically across evidence-strength levels (\S\ref{sec:direction_quality}), though 256-token truncation during GRPO training degrades this to approximately 0.60 (\S\ref{sec:cosine_failure}).
These results point to an appealing possibility: if the model's representations already separate sycophantic from non-sycophantic behavior, that separation should be convertible into a training signal.
Sycophancy is among the most persistent alignment failures in deployed systems \citep{sharma2023sycophancy}, and a representation-level signal could target the internal computation rather than its surface outputs.

This paper documents the \emph{probe reward trap}: when a frozen linear probe on $\dsyc$ is used as an SFT training signal with stopped gradients, behavioral death ($\tof = 0$) occurs within 500 steps while generation entropy remains healthy (0.70), masking the failure from standard monitoring (\S\ref{sec:probe_trap}).
In our experiments, the 1{,}300-step lag before distributional collapse means entropy-based early stopping---the most common safeguard against reward hacking \citep{casper2023openproblems}---would miss the failure entirely, with the reward averaging $+0.72$ throughout.
Because the trap arises under SFT rather than GRPO, it reflects a limitation of $\dsyc$ itself: the direction encodes \emph{whether} belief changed, not \emph{whether it should have}, so any reward conditioned on it alone will either be gamed or reward rigidity.

Under our GRPO configuration (Qwen3-8B, group size$=$2), two additional $\dsyc$-based formulations---cosine projection (\S\ref{sec:cosine_failure}) and continuous probe---also produced behavioral collapse.
Removing $\dsyc$ entirely, $\rthree$-only GRPO (behavioral reward alone) exceeded vanilla at only 4 of 28 checkpoints across two seeds; increasing group size to 8 does not improve performance ($\sycon = 0.085$, below vanilla).
ACT \citep{consistency2025bctact} (dense per-token SFT) exceeds vanilla at every evaluated checkpoint (32/32 across two seeds; \S\ref{sec:discussion}), and a LoRA-controlled ablation isolates supervision granularity as the primary factor.

The root cause is a semantic gap between discriminability and reward utility.
Techniques for discovering latent knowledge \citep{burns2023ccs} and representation-guided RL \citep{zhang2026latentgrpo} share a premise: a direction with high discriminability should transfer into a useful training signal.
For reasoning faithfulness and safety directions, this premise holds because the behavior to suppress is geometrically distinct from the behavior to preserve.
Sycophancy violates this condition: capitulation under social pressure and revision under valid evidence produce overlapping activation signatures along $\dsyc$ \citep{wang2025internal, shapira2026amplifies}.
When reward overoptimization \citep{gao2023scaling} operates on a signal that conflates compliance with capitulation, the result is predictable collapse \citep{skalse2022hacking}.

This paper presents a negative result with mechanistic analysis. Our two principal findings:

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{The probe reward trap: behavioral death before distributional collapse} (C2). A frozen binary probe on $\dsyc$ produces behavioral death ($\tof = 0$ at step 500) while entropy remains at 0.70 and the reward averages $+0.72$. In our experiments, the 1{,}300-step lag before distributional collapse renders standard entropy monitoring blind to the failure. Because the trap arises under SFT---not GRPO---it reflects a limitation of the direction itself, not the optimization algorithm (\S\ref{sec:probe_trap}).

\item \textbf{Scalar per-completion RL fails; supervision granularity is the primary factor} (C1). Under GRPO on Qwen3-8B, all three $\dsyc$-based reward formulations produce behavioral collapse (\S\ref{sec:cosine_failure}, \S\ref{sec:probe_trap}), and $\rthree$-only GRPO also fails (4/28 checkpoints ${>}$ vanilla). A group-size ablation (gs$=$8) rules out variance reduction as the bottleneck; a LoRA-controlled comparison demonstrates that per-token SFT ($\sycon{=}0.267$) exceeds per-completion GRPO ($\sycon{=}0.085$) by $3.1{\times}$ under identical adapter configurations (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).
\end{itemize}

\section{When Does Discriminability Fail as Reward Utility?}\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Root cause of the probe reward trap.}
The probe reward trap (\S\ref{sec:probe_trap}) and the cosine failures (\S\ref{sec:cosine_failure}) share a common geometric root.
$\dsyc$ encodes the \emph{direction} of belief change but not its \emph{evidential warrant}: valid revision and sycophantic capitulation both shift activations toward the user's position along the same direction.
The two reward families expose complementary faces of this blindness.
Cosine $\rone$ penalizes all belief change indiscriminately; the resulting mode collapse (F1c, F1d) reflects excessive punishment of any activation shift along $\dsyc$.
The binary probe $\rone$ rewards all resistance regardless of input validity; the stubbornness trap ($\tof = 0$ by step 500) reflects excessive permissiveness toward activation stasis.
These are not independent design flaws but dual consequences of a direction that conflates the target behavior (resisting invalid challenges) with its complement (refusing valid corrections).
Cross-model evidence confirms the limitation extends beyond Qwen3-8B: Llama-3-8B independently achieves AUROC $0.779$ (bootstrap 95\% CI $[0.745,\, 0.819]$) on the same contrastive pairs with the same monotonic evidence gradient, so discriminability generalizes across architectures while the semantic gap between discriminability and reward utility persists.
This pattern contrasts with reasoning faithfulness and safety directions~\citep{zhang2026latentgrpo}, where the behavior to suppress is geometrically distinct from the behavior to preserve along the relevant direction.
\citet{wu2026rewardhacking} reinforce this principle: concept directions applied via advantage modification in GRPO achieve 100\% validation accuracy for reward hacking detection, where shortcut behaviors are geometrically separable.
A quantitative comparison of geometric separability between $\dsyc$ and their reward-hacking directions remains an important open question.
For sycophancy, the target and its complement occupy the same activation region; they differ only in whether external evidence warrants the belief change.

\paragraph{GRPO results under our configuration.}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Comparison of all sycophancy calibration methods on Qwen3-8B. $\sycon$ is the harmonic mean of $\tof$ and $\nof$; higher indicates better calibration. Best result in \textbf{bold}. $^\dagger$Best checkpoint (seed 1, step 6500); only 4/28 checkpoints across two seeds exceed vanilla. $^\ddagger$Seed 2 (16 checkpoints); all exceed vanilla. Best $\sycon{=}0.286$ (step 7000). $^\S$All cosine variants collapsed from step 1 ($\tof{=}0$ at every checkpoint); F1d additionally diverged at step 2160 (entropy ${<}\,0.01$). $^\P$ACT and ActAdd differ from GRPO along 5+ dimensions (\S\ref{sec:discussion}); included for context, not as controlled comparisons.}
\label{tab:main_comparison}
\begin{tabular}{llcccc}
\toprule
Method & Type & $\sycon$ $\uparrow$ & $\tof$ $\uparrow$ & $\nof$ $\uparrow$ & Step \\
\midrule
Vanilla & -- & 0.134 & 0.072 & 0.945 & -- \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{6}{l}{\textit{GRPO with $\dsyc$}} \\
Cosine $\rone$ (F1a--F1d) & RL & 0.000$^\S$ & 0.000 & 1.000 & 500 \\
Continuous Probe $\rone$ (F3) & RL & 0.124 & 0.066 & 0.934 & 500 \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{6}{l}{\textit{SFT with $\dsyc$ probe penalty}} \\
Binary Probe $\rone$ (F2) & SFT & 0.000 & 0.000 & 0.995 & 500 \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{6}{l}{\textit{GRPO without $\dsyc$}} \\
$\rthree$-only GRPO & RL & 0.153$^\dagger$ & 0.083 & 0.983 & 6500 \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{6}{l}{\textit{Reference methods (not directly comparable)$^\P$}} \\
ActAdd ($\alpha{=}5$) & Inference & 0.054 & 0.028 & 0.961 & -- \\
\textbf{ACT} (seed 1) & SFT & \textbf{0.301} & \textbf{0.182} & 0.867 & 8000 \\
ACT (seed 2)$^\ddagger$ & SFT & 0.286 & -- & -- & 7000 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Table~\ref{tab:main_comparison} summarizes all methods evaluated on Qwen3-8B.
$\rthree$-only GRPO removes $\dsyc$ entirely and relies on the NLI-based behavioral reward alone.
If the failures in Sections~\ref{sec:cosine_failure} and~\ref{sec:probe_trap} stemmed solely from the representation reward, this ablation should recover calibration quality.
It does not.
The $\sycon$ trajectory for $\rthree$-only GRPO oscillates without sustained improvement.
Seed 1 peaks at 0.153 (checkpoint 6500) and ends at 0.143 (checkpoint 8000); seed 2 peaks at 0.143 (checkpoint 4000, its only checkpoint exceeding vanilla) and ends at 0.124 (checkpoint 8000).
Only 4 of 28 checkpoints across both seeds exceed vanilla (14.3\%): 3/12 for seed 1 (25\%) and 1/16 for seed 2 (6.3\%), while ACT exceeds vanilla at every evaluated checkpoint (32/32 across two seeds; Figure~\ref{fig:trajectory}).
Both seeds exhibit oscillations of similar amplitude ($\Delta \approx 0.069$) with crash onset differing by ${\sim}2{,}500$ steps, indicating stochastic drift in a saturated reward landscape.
Activation analysis confirms the drift is not representational: $\dsyc$ AUROC varies by ${<}0.01$ across checkpoints and $\rthree$ saturates at ${\sim}0.98$ ($p{=}0.703$), yet $\sycon$ swings by 17\%, reinforcing the disconnect between discriminability and behavioral utility.
Under our configuration (group size$=$2), $\rthree$-only GRPO exhibits a similar stubbornness pattern to the $\dsyc$ approaches (high $\nof$, near-zero $\tof$) at milder severity.

\paragraph{Competing hypotheses and ablation.}
Three explanations are consistent with our GRPO results: (a)~$\dsyc$ is fundamentally unsuitable as a reward signal for sycophancy calibration; (b)~GRPO with group size$=$2 provides insufficient ranking diversity for any reward to achieve stable calibration; (c)~sycophancy calibration is inherently unsuitable for scalar per-completion RL.
Two ablations address these hypotheses (Table~\ref{tab:ablation}).
Increasing group size from 2 to 8 does not improve $\rthree$-only GRPO: three checkpoints showed a monotonically declining trajectory ($0.084 \to 0.085 \to 0.054$), all below vanilla, and gs$=$8 (best 0.085) underperforms gs$=$2 (best 0.153); the experiment was terminated early.
This rules out hypothesis~(b) as the primary explanation.
Reducing ACT's LoRA configuration to match GRPO's (rank 64, $\alpha{=}64$, 4 modules) yields $\sycon = 0.267$ (peak 0.326 at step 7000); all 16 checkpoints exceed vanilla.
Under identical LoRA configurations, per-token SFT ($\sycon{=}0.267$) exceeds per-completion GRPO ($\sycon{=}0.153$) by $1.7{\times}$; supervision granularity is the primary driver, while LoRA capacity modulates convergence rate but is not the determining factor.
The probe reward trap (C2) provides independent evidence for~(a): it arises under SFT where group size is irrelevant.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Ablation: isolating supervision paradigm from LoRA configuration. All methods use Qwen3-8B with $\rthree$ (behavioral reward). Vanilla $\sycon{=}0.134$. $^\dagger$Terminated early after three checkpoints showed monotonically declining trajectory. $^\ddagger$Final checkpoint (step 8000); peak $\sycon{=}0.326$ at step 7000.}
\label{tab:ablation}
\begin{tabular}{llcc}
\toprule
Method & LoRA config & Best $\sycon$ & ${>}$Van. \\
\midrule
GRPO gs$=$2 (2 seeds) & r64, $\alpha$64, 4m & 0.153 & 4/28 \\
GRPO gs$=$8$^\dagger$ & r64, $\alpha$64, 4m & 0.085 & 0/3 \\
\midrule
ACT reduced-LoRA$^\ddagger$ & r64, $\alpha$64, 4m & 0.267 & 16/16 \\
ACT full s1 & r64, $\alpha$128, 7m & 0.301 & 16/16 \\
ACT full s2 & r64, $\alpha$128, 7m & 0.286 & 16/16 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/fig_trajectory.pdf}
\caption{$\sycon$ trajectories for $\rthree$-only GRPO (two seeds) and ACT (two seeds) over training steps. ACT exceeds vanilla at every evaluated checkpoint (32/32 across two seeds); $\rthree$-only GRPO exceeds vanilla at only 4/28 checkpoints (14.3\%).}
\label{fig:trajectory}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{ACT vs.\ GRPO.}
ACT~\citep{consistency2025bctact} achieves $\sycon = 0.301$ (seed 1) and $0.286$ (seed 2) at their respective peaks, more than $2{\times}$ vanilla and above every GRPO variant (Table~\ref{tab:main_comparison}) (held-out validation confirms generalization; see Limitations).
The trajectory is not monotonic---seed 1 dips to 0.214 at step 4000 but self-recovers by step 6000, unlike GRPO where stubbornness persists.
Full ACT peaks around steps 7000--8000 while reduced-LoRA surges to 0.326 at step 7000; both variants maintain above-vanilla performance throughout.
The reduced-LoRA ablation (Table~\ref{tab:ablation}) partially disentangles the five confounding dimensions: with LoRA capacity controlled, per-token SFT still dominates, indicating that supervision granularity---not adapter capacity---is the primary factor.

\paragraph{Relationship to inference-time probe methods.}
\citet{papadatos2024probepenalties} successfully reduce sycophancy using a probe of comparable quality (94\% accuracy) via Best-of-N reranking, where the probe selects among candidates without producing gradients.
Together with our results, this suggests two orthogonal failure dimensions: (1)~inside vs.\ outside the optimization loop---gradient exploitation enables the probe reward trap (\S\ref{sec:probe_trap}), while inference-time reranking sidesteps it; and (2)~scalar per-completion reward---the failure persists even without the probe ($\rthree$-only GRPO), consistent with per-completion information compression as an independent factor.

\paragraph{Future directions.}
Condition-aware rewards, hybrid SFT-then-RL pipelines, and per-step process rewards offer paths forward; whether other REINFORCE-style methods or behavioral attributes with similar geometric entanglement~\citep{skalse2022hacking} exhibit the same failures remains open.
